stages.ingestion: Each round the tool response (search results, a goal-directed page summary, or code output) enters the workspace as the only raw observation.
stages.construction: The policy writes a structured decision: a think trace, a full new report of all findings so far, and one action (tool call or answer).
stages.organization: The workspace always has four parts: question, report, last tool call, last tool response.
stages.update: The next workspace is rebuilt from the question, the new report and the latest exchange; earlier rounds and the think trace are discarded.
stages.answer: The policy answers from the workspace when it judges the information sufficient, or is forced to answer in the last allowed round (released code).
stages.learning: Rejection-sampling SFT on 110K synthesized trajectories, then EAPO: GSPO with geometrically discounted rewards (gamma 0.995) over per-round samples and adaptive downsampling.

summary: Deep-research agent that replaces a growing context with a per-round rebuilt workspace (question, a report the policy rewrites each round, last exchange), trained with an efficiency-discounted RL objective.
notes: Venue: ICLR 2026 poster (OpenReview venueid ICLR.cc/2026/Conference, forum qQ5MZ5Mx7p); arXiv v2 comment says camera-ready for ICLR 2026. Title changed from v1 ('...via Markovian State Reconstruction') to 'Rethinking Long-Horizon Agents with Interaction Scaling' in v2/ICLR. headline: The memory is one report that the policy rewrites in full every round; everything else from earlier rounds is dropped.
Nothing is retrieved: the policy always reads the whole workspace (question, report, last call, last response).
The report's size is never reported; it is bounded only by what the trained policy chooses to write.

discussion.takeaway: Rebuilding the agent's context each round around a self-written report, instead of appending every step, lets a 30B MoE deep-research agent keep improving with more turns; in the authors' tests it beats open-source agents on six benchmarks and helps frontier models as a prompt.

claims.claim: Best open-source deep-research agent on six benchmarks.
claims.evidence: Average +14.5pp over the best open-source agent: HLE 28.8, BC 37.3, BC-zh 45.2, GAIA 72.8, Xbench-DS 71.0, SEAL-0 39.6. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: The iterative workspace beats a growing context under the same training data.
claims.evidence: Average 49.1 vs 36.5 for Mono-Agent (which had 64K context vs 40K). Table 2, §4.3

claims.claim: Accuracy keeps rising with more allowed turns.
claims.evidence: BrowseComp-200: 3.5% at 2 turns to 42.5% at 2048, trained with Tmax 32. Fig. 3, App. B.3

claims.claim: Works as a prompting strategy without training.
claims.evidence: BrowseComp over ReAct: o3 49.7 → 62.4 (+12.7), DeepSeek-V3.1 30.0 → 49.2 (+19.2). Fig. 4

claims.claim: The discounted reward makes exploration shorter at similar accuracy.

discussion.limits_src: not stated: the paper has no limitations section
reading: Nothing bounds the report except the trained policy; the paper never reports report lengths, so the O(1) workspace claim is untested in numbers.

The text and Fig. 3 disagree: the text says 5.5% → 50.1% and 80.1 average turns at 2048, the figure and abstract say 3.5% → 42.5% and 129.5 turns; App. B.3 cites 15.2% at Tmax 32 where the figure shows 23.5.
App. C.3 says Table 1 baseline numbers were taken from the original papers, so tools, search back-ends and turn budgets differ from IterResearch's (which uses Tmax up to 256).
The Mono-Agent ablation changes paradigm and context length (64K vs 40K) together; it is the fairest comparison in the paper but not a single-variable one.
The 'last tool response' is often already a summary: Visit returns a helper LLM's goal-directed extract of the page, not the page.
The released code is a reproduction with different tools, so the reported numbers cannot be traced to code.

abstract.text: IterResearch targets long-horizon deep-research agents, which usually append every search result and thought to one growing context until it fills with noise. Instead, each round the agent works from a small rebuilt workspace: the question, a report it rewrites itself to hold all findings, and only the latest tool call and response. A 30B MoE model is trained for this with rejection-sampling SFT and an RL objective whose rewards are discounted by trajectory length. The authors report large gains over open-source agents on six benchmarks, accuracy that keeps rising up to 2048 turns, and gains for o3 and DeepSeek-V3.1 when the scheme is used only as a prompt.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.
